weight-class.short: The U number is the frame's weight band — smaller U means heavier: 3U (85–89g) is heaviest, then 4U, 5U, 6U (70–74g) the lightest.
weight-class.long: Badminton frames are graded by weight in "U" classes. Confusingly, a smaller number is heavier: 3U ≈ 85–89g, 4U ≈ 80–84g, 5U ≈ 75–79g, 6U ≈ 70–74g. Heavier frames put more mass behind a smash but are slower to swing and more tiring in fast exchanges; lighter frames are quicker to react and defend with, but need cleaner timing to generate power.

balance-point.short: Distance from the handle to the frame's balance point in mm — higher number = more weight in the head = more power, slower swing.
balance-point.long: Balance point is where the racket balances along its length, measured in millimetres from the butt cap. A higher number means weight sits further toward the head (head-heavy: more power, slower to swing). A lower number means weight sits toward the handle (head-light: faster, easier to defend and block with). We treat the measured balance point — not the printed label — as the source of truth, because the two occasionally disagree in the spec sheet.

balance-label.short: Head-Heavy, Even, or Head-Light — a plain-language reading of where the weight sits. The measured balance point is the precise version.
balance-label.long: The balance label summarises the balance point: Head-Heavy (power-oriented), Even Balance (all-round), or Head-Light (speed and defence). It's a quick read; for exact comparisons use the balance-point number in millimetres.

shaft-stiffness.short: How much the shaft flexes on contact — stiffer shafts reward fast, clean swings; softer shafts add repulsion and forgiveness.
shaft-stiffness.long: The shaft is the thin tube between the handle and the head. A stiff shaft flexes little and returns energy fast, which suits players with quick, well-timed swings and gives a crisp, controlled feel. A softer (more flexible) shaft loads and springs back to add power for slower swings, and is more forgiving of imperfect timing, at the cost of a little control. We show the measured stiffness range as the primary number and the word (Soft…Stiff) as a label.

shaft-diameter.short: How thick the shaft is in mm — thinner shafts cut through the air faster; thicker shafts are more stable on hard hits.
shaft-diameter.long: Shaft diameter, in millimetres, trades air resistance against stability. A thinner shaft (around 6.2–6.6mm) slices through the air for faster swings and quick flat exchanges. A thicker shaft (around 6.8–7.0mm) is more stable and planted on powerful smashes and off-centre hits.

frame-holes.short: How many string holes the frame has — more holes can mean a denser, more controlled string bed; the pattern also affects feel.
frame-holes.long: The number and layout of grommet holes in the frame shape the string bed. More holes and slanted patterns can support a denser, more controlled bed and a larger sweet spot, while the exact feel depends on how the frame and stringing interact. Treat it as a construction detail, not a headline spec.

frame-area.short: The area of the string face in cm² — a larger face is more forgiving on off-centre hits; a smaller face can feel more precise.
frame-area.long: Frame (string-face) area, in square centimetres, roughly tracks the size of the hitting surface. A larger area is more forgiving of mishits with a bigger sweet spot; a smaller, more compact head can feel more precise and cut through the air a touch faster. Some models in this lineup don't publish this figure, in which case we show a dash.

grip-size.short: How thick the handle is — G6 is smaller (thinner), G5 is larger (thicker). Grip your natural finger wrap prefers.
grip-size.long: Grip size describes the handle thickness. In this lineup G6 is the smaller (thinner) handle and G5 is the larger (thicker) one. A grip that's too small encourages over-gripping; too large limits wrist snap. You can always build a thinner grip up with an overgrip, so many players size down when unsure.

max-tension.short: The highest safe stringing tension for the frame in lbs — a ceiling, NOT a recommended tension. String below it for durability.
max-tension.long: Max tension is the manufacturer's ceiling for how tightly the frame can be strung, in pounds. It is a safety limit, not a suggestion — stringing at the maximum every time shortens frame life and demands very clean contact. Higher tension gives a flatter, more controlled response for advanced players; lower tension adds repulsion and forgiveness. Pick a tension your technique supports, comfortably under this number.

swing-weight.short: How heavy the racket feels while swinging (not its static weight) — higher swing weight hits harder but is more tiring and slower.
swing-weight.long: Swing weight measures how heavy the racket feels in motion, accounting for how its mass is distributed, not just the number on the scale. A higher swing weight carries more momentum into the shuttle for heavier smashes, but is slower to manoeuvre and more tiring over a long match. Some models in this lineup don't publish a swing weight, shown here as a dash.

classification.short: OGKILS's play-style grade for the frame: ATTACK (power), SPEED (fast/flat), CONTROL (placement), or ALL-AROUND (balanced).
classification.long: Classification is OGKILS's own summary of what a frame is built for. ATTACK frames are head-heavy and reward smashing. SPEED frames favour fast, flat exchanges and quick defence. CONTROL frames prioritise placement and a steady feel. ALL-AROUND frames sit in the middle and adapt to most situations — a safe default if you're unsure.
